column4: The challenge asks from what thing the human was created, opening the sequence whose next ayah answers with sperm, creation, and measure.
After the measured origin and eased way of 80:19-20, Allah causes the human to die and be buried; the bodily sequence is carried to its earthly end.
After death and burial, Allah raises the human whenever He wills, completing the fetus-to-resurrection arc in 80:18-22.
We created you, so why do you not affirm the truth, introduces the reproductive-fluid questions of 56:58-59 and makes created embodiment their premise.
Allah is the One who causes death and gives life; 53:45-46 then locate the male-female pair in emitted sperm, so the life-and-death claim frames bodily generation.
The other or final bringing-forth belongs to Allah, completing 53:44-46's movement from life and death through sperm-born sex to renewed creation.
The wife of Imran dedicates what is in her womb to her Lord, placing the still-hidden child within divine nurture before the delivery and growth narrated in 3:36-37.
At delivery the mother identifies the child as female, names her Mary, and entrusts her offspring to Allah; the hidden womb of 3:35 becomes a born and sexed child whom 3:37 then causes to grow.
Allah announces that He is creating a human from clay, supplying the bodily referent that 15:29 then proportions and breathes into.
Allah announces creation of a human from clay; 38:72 contributes the subsequent proportioning and animation, so this ayah states the material beginning of that formed body.
When Joseph reaches full strength, Allah gives him judgment and knowledge; it is a repeated formulation of mature bodily arrival, though without 28:14's additional word for full development.
Two complete years of nursing are set for one who wishes to complete suckling, while the father bears provision; early bodily growth is given a measured duration and sustained by parental care.
The infant Moses is carried by the water under divine protection and is to be formed under Allah's eye; the child is both physically preserved and deliberately brought through an early stage.

The ayah sets waiting terms for those past menstruation, those not yet menstruating, and pregnant women whose term ends at delivery; reproductive stages and their bodily boundary are measured together.
Children who reach puberty move to the adult rule of seeking permission, making bodily maturation a definite threshold in the life course.
Allah creates the human from water and then establishes ties of blood and marriage, extending bodily origin into generational kinship.
Were humans created from nothing, or are they themselves the creators, isolates divine forming agency in a way parallel to the question over who creates the emitted fluid in 56:58-59.
Revived earth is offered as evidence that the same giver of life revives the dead and is powerful over everything; pasture, resurrection, and the power sense of ق د ر meet directly.
Rain makes the humbled earth stir and swell, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead; the growing-ground analogue leads explicitly to bodily return and divine power.

Water descends from heaven in due measure, revives a dead land, and is followed by the statement that humans will likewise be brought out; measured fluid, growth, and resurrection form one comparison.
The Creator who was not wearied by creating the heavens and earth is declared able to revive the dead, giving another explicit resurrection use of the power sense of the section's ق د ر family.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is asked whether He is able to create the like of decomposed humans; the affirmative answer joins divine power to bodily re-creation.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is able to create the like of the objectors and has appointed their term, combining re-creative power with a measured lifespan.
The offender who comes to his Lord faces hell where he neither dies nor lives, exactly repeating the bodily boundary between death and life stated in 87:13 and showing its punitive sense.

The transgressor prefers the worldly life, repeating the stance and wording of 87:16; against this section's womb-to-old-age arc, the developed person's decisive preference becomes another life stage.
These people prefer worldly life over the Hereafter, a repeated formulation of the choice in 87:16-17 and the ethical outcome of the bodily lifetime traced by the section.
Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter and turn others from Allah's way enact the same preference named in 87:16, here joined to active distortion of guidance.

Wealth and children are called the adornment of worldly life immediately after 18:45's withering vegetation; human offspring are thus named within the garden image paired with the formed man of 18:37.

Water is sent down in measure and lodged in the earth, a deliberate structural parallel to reproductive fluid lodged in a secure womb; here the measured deposit sustains the growing ground and can also be withdrawn.

The Hour makes every nursing mother neglect her infant and every pregnant female cast off her burden; ordinary nurture and gestational completion are violently interrupted, defining the bodily order's catastrophic boundary.
Elderly women beyond expectation of marriage occupy a stated reproductive and social boundary, complementing the section's movement from bodily maturity into old age.

The human is asked what has deceived him concerning his generous Lord; 82:7-8 answer by recalling his creation, proportioning, balance, and chosen form, so this ayah frames the ordered body as grounds for accountability.

Everything's treasuries belong to Allah and it is sent down only in a known measure; without specifying the body, the ayah gives provision the same exact apportioning that governs gestation in the section.

A crop sends out shoots, strengthens them, grows thick, and stands on its stalk, a staged maturation applied to the believing community that indirectly illuminates the section's child-and-pasture meeting.

Love of women, sons, livestock, and cultivated land is presented together as the enjoyment of worldly life; reproduction, offspring, pasture, and dunya meet within one inventory of transient attachment.
Moses' mother is told to nurse her newborn and promised his return, adding the vulnerable nourishment immediately after birth to the section's account of a child being raised stage by stage.
Orphans are tested until marriageable age and the appearance of sound judgment, making growth into adult capacity a practical threshold rather than an undifferentiated span.
